newsitem.title: USA: Clinton lead over Dole 12.8 percent - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton lead over Dole 12.8 percent - Reuters poll.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's lead over Republican Bob Dole narrowed slightly to 12.8 percent in a Reuters poll released on Wednesday.

Clinton got 45.8 percent support to Dole's 33 percent in the poll, conducted for Reuters by John Zogby Group International. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot had 5.1 percent, 2.9 percent picked "other" and 13.1 percent are still undecided.

Pollster John Zogby noted that the results broke an eight-day streak in which Clinton's lead had increased daily in the Reuters poll, peaking at 15.1 percent before it tightened to 12.8 percent on Wednesday.
"One day doesn't make a trend. But it really does seem to me we are not talking about a 20-point race, under any circumstances," Zogby said.
Another survey released on Wednesday, the CNN/Gallup poll, also pointed to a narrowing of the race, placing Clinton just nine points ahead with 48 percent to Dole's 39 percent.
But a new ABC News poll said Wednesday the gap was 17 points: 55 percent for Clinton, 38 percent for Dole.
Zogby said that after the second Clinton/Dole debate in San Diego on Wednesday night, "I suspect we'll probably see things settle into the high single digits or low double digits."

The Reuters/Zogby poll tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, is a rolling average of polling from Sunday through Tuesday.

Most of the polling was completed before Dole's speech on Tuesday in which the Republican unleashed his broadest attack yet on Clinton, but Zogby said "it doesn't appear that this tactic is going to move mountains" for Dole.
He said he thought the main impact from the speech "might be to shore up Republicans."

In the battle for Congress Democrats continued to lead with 38.5 percent to 33 percent for Republicans when voters were asked which party's candidate they intended to support in their congressional district.

But Democrats and Republicans were in a dead heat when voters were asked their preferred party to rule the Senate -- 40.4 percent Democrat to 40 percent Republican. The Democrats kept a small edge as the party favoured to take control of the House, 40.8 percent to 37.5 percent.

Zogby said his rule is that if Clinton's margin is 13 percentage points or more, Clinton has the potential to help the Democrats take back majority control of both houses of Congress from Republicans.
If the election for president were held today, for whom would you vote, Clinton, Dole, or Perot?
